stimuli.title: Passage I
stimuli.text:
Read the passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

Every year, somewhere between November and March, the harmattan arrives in northern Nigeria like an uninvited guest who knows he will be tolerated. The dry wind blows down from the Sahara, carrying a fine dust that settles on roofs, cars and window ledges. By mid-morning the sun is a pale disc, more like a moon than a source of heat, and distant hills disappear into a grey haze.

The season brings its own hardships. Lips crack, skin turns ashy and dry, and coughs travel from house to house. Pilots and drivers dread the low visibility, for a road that is clear at noon can be blinded by dust an hour later. Farmers, too, watch anxiously as the wind strips moisture from the soil.

Yet the harmattan is not without its gifts. The cool mornings are a relief after the heat of the rainy season, and clothes spread out in the compound dry within an hour. Many people say the season sharpens the appetite and lifts the spirit, since it coincides with the festive end of the year. Children who shiver at dawn are racing around the compound by afternoon. To those who have grown up with it, the harmattan is less an enemy than an old, difficult relative: tiresome, but missed when it is gone.

stimuli.title: Passage II
stimuli.text:
Read the passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

Emeka had never thought much of his grandmother's stall at Ogbete Market until the day she fell ill and handed him the key. "Open at seven," she said from her bed, "and do not argue with Mama Chidi about the price of crayfish. She always wins."

By eight o'clock Emeka understood why his grandmother came home so tired. Customers did not simply buy; they bargained, complained, asked after relatives he had never met and promised to pay tomorrow. A woman in a blue wrapper picked up every tomato in the basket before buying three. A boy ran off with a sachet of pepper and Emeka, weighed down by the sacks around him, could only watch him go.

At noon Mama Chidi arrived. Emeka squared his shoulders and named a price. She laughed, a long, warm laugh that drew the attention of the whole row, and then she paid it without a word. "Tell your grandmother," she said, "that the boy will do."

That evening Emeka counted the day's takings twice and found that he had made less than his grandmother usually did. Still, when he gave her the money, she held his hand longer than he expected. He had learnt that a market is not only a place where things are sold.

stimuli.title: Passage III
stimuli.text:
Read the passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

Should secondary school students be allowed to carry mobile phones to school? Many principals answer with a firm no, and their reasons deserve respect. Phones distract students in class, encourage cheating in examinations and expose young people to bullying and unsuitable content. A ban, they argue, is simple to enforce and protects learning time.

However, a total ban treats the phone as the problem rather than the way it is used. For a student in a crowded city, a phone may be the only way to reach a parent when a bus breaks down or a lesson ends late. In schools with poorly stocked libraries, the same device can open a world of dictionaries, encyclopaedias and past lessons. To forbid it entirely is to throw away a tool that many families have made sacrifices to buy.

A wiser policy lies between the two extremes. Phones could be switched off and kept in bags during lessons, used only with a teacher's permission and never taken into an examination hall. Students who break the rules would lose the privilege. Such a policy is harder to manage than a ban, but it teaches something no ban can teach: self-control. After all, these students will soon leave school for a world in which no principal will be there to take their phones away.

stimuli.title: Cloze passage
stimuli.text:
In the passage below, the numbered gaps show where words have been left out. For each gap, choose the option that best completes it.

Walk through any busy Nigerian city and you will see plastic bottles and nylon bags in gutters and drains. When the rains come, this waste ......(1)...... the drains, and the water spills into streets and homes. For years the problem seemed too large to ......(2)......, but a number of young people have begun to see waste not as a nuisance but as a ......(3)...... .

In several cities, small recycling firms now pay collectors for every kilogram of plastic they bring in. The plastic is sorted, cleaned and ......(4)...... into pellets, which factories use to make new products. Households that once threw bottles into the street now keep them in sacks, knowing they can be ......(5)...... for cash or household goods.

The ......(6)...... are easy to see. Drains flow more freely, fewer streets flood and hundreds of young people have found ......(7)...... . Yet recycling alone cannot solve the problem. Manufacturers must be ......(8)...... to use less packaging, and citizens must stop buying more plastic than they need. A clean city is not the work of one ......(9)...... but of everyone who lives in it, and its benefits, too, are ......(10)...... by all.

stimuli.title: Passage I
stimuli.text:
Read the passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

Along the river valleys of northern Nigeria lie stretches of low, flat land that flood during the rainy season. Farmers call these lands fadama. When the floodwater recedes, it leaves behind soil that stays moist long after the surrounding plains have turned brown and hard.

For generations, farmers have used this moisture to grow a second crop in the dry season. Where the soil begins to dry, they draw water from shallow wells or from the river itself, once with buckets and calabashes and now often with small pumps. Tomatoes, onions, peppers and leafy vegetables flourish under the strong dry-season sun, and because they reach the market when little else is being harvested, they fetch good prices.

Dry-season farming has other advantages. It keeps young people employed in months that would otherwise be idle, and it reduces the pressure on them to drift to the cities in search of work. It also spreads a family's income across the year, so that a poor rainy season need not mean hunger.

The practice is not free of risk. Pumps are costly to run, wells can fail, and the same land may be wanted by herders whose animals need water and grazing. Careful planning, and agreements between farmers and herders, are needed if the valleys are to feed everyone who depends on them.

stimuli.title: Passage II
stimuli.text:
Read the passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

The bus left Enugu at dawn, full of traders, students and a goat whose owner insisted it was travelling to a wedding. For the first two hours everyone was cheerful. A preacher at the front sang hymns; a man at the back sold medicine that, he claimed, could cure anything from headaches to bad luck.

Then, somewhere past Onitsha, the engine coughed, spluttered and died. The driver climbed down, opened the bonnet and stared into it with the expression of a man reading a letter in a language he did not know. Passengers spilled onto the roadside. Some complained loudly; others bought roasted corn from girls who seemed to appear from nowhere.

Ifeoma, who was going to Lagos to begin her university course, sat on her box and watched the sun climb. At first she fretted about arriving late. But as the hours passed, she found herself talking with an old woman who had made the same journey forty years before, when the road was narrower and the buses slower. By the time a mechanic arrived on a motorcycle and coaxed the engine back to life, Ifeoma had stopped worrying. The journey, she decided, had already taught her more than she had expected to learn in her first week of lectures.

stimuli.title: Passage III
stimuli.text:
Read the passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

In which language should a child first learn to read? Many educators argue that the answer is obvious: the language the child speaks at home. A pupil who is taught in a familiar language can concentrate on new ideas instead of struggling with unfamiliar words. Research in many countries suggests that children who first master reading in their mother tongue later learn a second language more easily, not less.

Opponents of this view raise practical objections. Nigeria has hundreds of languages, and a single classroom in a city may contain children who speak five or six of them. Textbooks in many of these languages do not exist, and teachers trained to teach in them are few. Parents, too, often want their children taught in English from the first day, believing that English is the key to examinations, jobs and success.

These objections are real, but they are arguments for careful planning, not for abandoning the idea. Where a community shares one language, early lessons can be given in it while English is introduced step by step. Where it does not, schools can make English the medium of instruction while still valuing the languages children bring from home. What matters most is that no child should sit in a classroom for years, understanding little of what is said, simply because the adults around them never asked which language the child understood.

stimuli.title: Cloze passage
stimuli.text:
In the passage below, the numbered gaps show where words have been left out. For each gap, choose the option that best completes it.

The inter-house sports competition is the high point of the second term at our school. Weeks before the event, each house ......(1)...... its best athletes and begins training in the early mornings, long before the first lesson. Students who cannot run or jump find other ways to ......(2)......: they design banners, compose songs and practise the march past.

On the day itself, the field is ......(3)...... with colour. Parents and old students crowd the stands, and the noise of drums and whistles can be heard ......(4)...... away. The first event is usually the hundred metres, and the ......(5)...... of the girls' race often sets the mood for the rest of the day.

Not every moment is one of triumph. Some athletes stumble, others are ......(6)...... at the finishing line, and tears are shed. Yet the teachers remind us that the purpose of the day is not only to win but to learn ......(7)...... . A house that loses with dignity earns as much ......(8)...... as one that wins with arrogance.

When the last relay is over and the trophy has been ......(9)......, the field slowly empties. The banners are folded away, but the friendships formed on the training ground ......(10)...... long after the cheering has died down.

stimuli.title: Passage I
stimuli.text:
Read the passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

In many towns before the age of radio, news travelled on foot. The town crier walked from street to street at dusk, beating a gong and announcing the ruler's messages: a meeting at the palace, a day of communal labour, a warning about a thief seen near the stream. People gathered at their doorways to listen, and what they heard was repeated at the well and in the market the next morning.

The system had obvious limits. A message could reach only as far as the crier could walk, and it changed a little each time it was retold. Yet it had strengths that are easy to forget. The crier was a known figure, and his words carried the authority of the palace. Listeners could ask him questions, and he could see at once whether he had been understood.

Today a message can reach millions in seconds through a phone. But speed has brought its own dangers. False stories spread as quickly as true ones, and no one stands at the doorway to answer questions or take responsibility for what is said. Perhaps the modern listener needs some of the caution of the old one, who always asked, before repeating a message, who had sent it and why.

stimuli.title: Passage II
stimuli.text:
Read the passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

Musa was fifteen when his father took him to the workshop of Alhaji Danladi, the most respected carpenter in Zaria. The workshop smelt of sawdust and varnish, and its walls were hung with tools whose names Musa did not know.

For the first three months he was not allowed to touch a saw. He swept the floor, sharpened chisels and carried planks from the timber shed. When he complained to his mother, she reminded him that a tree does not bear fruit in the season it is planted. Musa was not comforted.

One afternoon a customer brought in a broken chair, an old piece made by Alhaji Danladi's own teacher. The master was away, and the other apprentices shrugged. Musa studied the chair for a long time. He had watched closely while he swept, and he knew how the joints should fit. Carefully, he cut a new rail, shaped it and glued it into place.

When Alhaji Danladi returned, he turned the chair over in his hands without speaking. Then he took a small chisel from the wall, the one he never lent to anyone, and gave it to Musa. "Tomorrow," he said, "you begin."

stimuli.title: Passage III
stimuli.text:
Read the passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

It is often said that Nigerians do not read. The charge is unfair. Visit any motor park and you will see drivers bent over newspapers; walk past a church or mosque and you will find people studying holy books with great care. What is lacking is not the desire to read but easy access to books.

In many communities, the nearest public library is far away, poorly lit and stocked with books older than the readers. Bookshops are found mainly in large cities, and books are expensive for families with many other needs. A child who finishes the only story book in the house has nowhere to find another.

If we want a reading nation, we must bring books to where people are. Small community libraries, run from a spare room in a school or a town hall, can do more than a grand building that few can reach. Mobile libraries can visit villages on market days. Schools can set aside time each week when every pupil, and every teacher, simply reads.

None of this requires great wealth. It requires the belief that reading is not a luxury for a few but a habit that every child can acquire, given the chance. The returns, in thoughtful citizens and capable workers, will repay the effort many times over.

stimuli.title: Cloze passage
stimuli.text:
In the passage below, the numbered gaps show where words have been left out. For each gap, choose the option that best completes it.

Long before banks reached every town, traders in Nigeria had their own ways of saving. One of the most common is the rotating contribution group. A number of people agree to ......(1)...... a fixed sum at regular intervals, and each time the whole amount is given to one member in ......(2)...... . Over time every member receives the collection once.

The system ......(3)...... on trust. There are no written contracts, and a member who collects early must continue to pay until the cycle is complete. A person who ......(4)...... on this duty quickly loses the respect of the community, and few groups will ......(5)...... such a person again.

For many families the contribution group is more than a way of saving. It ......(6)...... them to set money aside when it would be easy to spend it, and it gives each member a large sum at a time when it can be ......(7)...... wisely, perhaps to buy stock for a shop or pay school fees.

Today some groups keep their records on phones and ......(8)...... members by text message, but the ......(9)...... remains the same. In a world of complicated financial products, the contribution group is a reminder that ......(10)...... and discipline can achieve a great deal.

questions.stem: The passage is mainly about
options: the festivals at the end of every year
why pilots fear the dry season
questions.explanation: The first paragraph describes the season, the second its hardships and the third its gifts, so the passage weighs both sides. Crops, pilots and festivals are each mentioned only in passing.

questions.stem: "Like an uninvited guest who knows he will be tolerated" is an example of
questions.explanation: The comparison is made openly with "like", which makes it a simile. A metaphor would say the harmattan is a guest without "like" or "as".

questions.stem: According to the passage, drivers dread the harmattan because
options: the dust damages their car engines badly
questions.explanation: "A road that is clear at noon can be blinded by dust an hour later" shows that visibility can fall suddenly. Slippery roads and engine damage are not mentioned.

questions.stem: The word "coincides" as used in the passage means
questions.explanation: The season "coincides with the festive end of the year": the two happen at the same time. Nothing suggests that one follows or opposes the other.

questions.stem: The writer's final view of the harmattan is best described as
questions.explanation: Calling the harmattan "tiresome, but missed when it is gone" admits its faults while showing affection, so the view is fond but realistic. Nothing in the ending is bitter or indifferent.

questions.stem: Why did Emeka take charge of the stall?
questions.explanation: The first sentence says his grandmother "fell ill and handed him the key". There is no mention of a journey or of Emeka wanting money.

questions.stem: From the passage, it can be inferred that Mama Chidi
questions.explanation: She laughs, pays his price without argument and says "the boy will do", which shows she was judging how he handled her. Nothing suggests dislike, lack of money or interest in the stall.

questions.stem: "Squared his shoulders" as used in the passage suggests that Emeka
options: stood up to leave the stall at once
questions.explanation: To square one's shoulders is to straighten up before facing something difficult. Emeka was bracing himself to bargain with the woman who "always wins".

questions.stem: Emeka could not chase the boy who stole the pepper because
options: he did not see the theft
a customer was holding him by the arm
questions.explanation: The passage says Emeka was "weighed down by the sacks around him" and "could only watch him go". He saw the theft, so he did not miss it.

questions.stem: The last sentence suggests that Emeka learnt that a market is also
options: a place where children are cheated
questions.explanation: The customers ask after relatives, Mama Chidi judges his character and his grandmother holds his hand: the market is about people as well as trade. He made less money than usual, so wealth is not the lesson.

questions.stem: The writer's main argument is that schools should
questions.explanation: The third paragraph proposes "a wiser policy" between a ban and free use: phones switched off in lessons and used only with permission. The writer rejects both extremes.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT given in the passage as a reason for banning phones?
questions.explanation: The principals' reasons are distraction, cheating, bullying and unsuitable content. The cost of a phone appears only in the argument against a ban.

questions.stem: The tone of the passage is best described as
questions.explanation: The writer says the principals' reasons "deserve respect" before arguing for a middle way, which is balanced and persuasive. There is no anger, humour or regret.

questions.stem: "Throw away a tool" as used in the passage means to
questions.explanation: The phrase is figurative: banning phones wastes a device that can open "dictionaries, encyclopaedias and past lessons". No one literally throws anything.

questions.stem: The writer believes the proposed policy is better than a ban mainly because it
options: is easier for schools to manage
questions.explanation: The writer admits the policy "is harder to manage than a ban" but says it "teaches something no ban can teach: self-control". So ease of management is the opposite of what the passage says.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (1).
questions.explanation: Waste in the drains stops the water, which then "spills into streets and homes". Cleaning, widening or emptying the drains would do the opposite.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (2).
questions.explanation: A problem "too large to tackle" is one people felt unable to deal with. That sets up the contrast with the young people who have begun to act.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (3).
questions.explanation: "Not as a nuisance but as a ..." needs a word opposite in feeling to nuisance. A resource is something of value, which matches the paid collection in the next paragraph.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (4).
questions.explanation: Plastic that factories reuse has to be processed into pellets. Burying, burning or scattering it would leave nothing to sell.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (5).
questions.explanation: Households keep bottles "knowing they can be exchanged for cash or household goods". Only exchanged takes "for" with that meaning.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (6).
questions.explanation: The sentence lists good results: freer drains, fewer floods, new jobs. Those are benefits.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (7).
questions.explanation: Young people paid to collect and sort plastic have found employment, that is, work. The other nouns do not fit the economic sense of the paragraph.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (8).
questions.explanation: "Manufacturers must be urged to use less packaging", that is, pressed to do so. Forbidden and prevented would stop them using less, and excused reverses the sense.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (9).
questions.explanation: A clean city is not the work of one agency, a single organisation, "but of everyone". An agenda or an occasion cannot do work.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (10).
questions.explanation: The benefits of a clean city "are shared by all" who live in it, which completes the idea that everyone takes part.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"The new principal has promised to put the school's house in order."
options: He will repair the school buildings
He will sell the staff quarters
He will sort out its problems
questions.explanation: To put one's house in order is to sort out one's own affairs and problems. It has nothing to do with real buildings.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"Chika's father warned her that the chairman's offer was a mere flash in the pan."
questions.explanation: A flash in the pan is a sudden success or promise that soon fades and comes to nothing.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"When the results were announced, Bayo was on cloud nine."
questions.explanation: To be on cloud nine is to be extremely happy. The phrase says nothing about confusion or height.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"The councillor's speech fell on deaf ears."
options: It was too loud to follow
The audience could not hear well
questions.explanation: Words that fall on deaf ears are ignored. The audience heard them but did not heed them.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"Had the driver slowed down, the accident would not have happened."
options: The driver will slow down next time
The driver did not slow down
The driver slowed down too late
questions.explanation: "Had the driver slowed down" is a third conditional about the past that did not happen: he did not slow down, and the accident did happen.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The chairman's speech was so __verbose__ that many guests fell asleep.
questions.explanation: Verbose means using more words than are needed, that is, wordy. Brief is its opposite.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The farmers were __apprehensive__ about the late arrival of the rains.
questions.explanation: Apprehensive means anxious that something bad may happen.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The thief tried to __abscond__ with the church's offering.
questions.explanation: To abscond is to leave secretly, usually to escape with something taken.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

Her kindness to the orphans was __commendable__.
questions.explanation: Something commendable deserves praise.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The witness gave a __lucid__ account of the accident.
questions.explanation: A lucid account is clear and easy to understand.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The new teacher is very __lenient__ with latecomers.
questions.explanation: Lenient means tolerant and mild in punishing. Its opposite is strict. Kind and patient are close to lenient, not opposite.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The village is known for its __hospitable__ people.
questions.explanation: Hospitable means friendly and welcoming to guests, so the opposite is unfriendly.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The governor's visit was a __rare__ event in the village.
questions.explanation: Rare means not happening often; the opposite is common.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The witness's account was __consistent__ with the evidence.
questions.explanation: Consistent means in agreement. Contradictory means in conflict, the opposite.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The minister gave an __evasive__ answer to the reporter's question.
questions.explanation: An evasive answer avoids the question; a direct answer meets it head on.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

Neither the principal nor the teachers ...... aware of the change.
questions.explanation: With "neither ... nor", the verb agrees with the nearer subject. "The teachers" is plural, so "were".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

Nobody came to the meeting, ......?
questions.explanation: "Nobody" makes the sentence negative, so the tag is positive, and "they" is the standard pronoun for nobody: "did they?"

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

The new students were introduced ...... the staff on Monday.
questions.explanation: One is introduced to someone. "Introduced with" is a common error.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

By the time the police arrived, the robbers ......
questions.explanation: An action completed before another past action takes the past perfect: "had escaped".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

Of the two sisters, Kemi is the ......
questions.explanation: When only two are compared, the comparative is used: "the taller of the two".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

The prize was shared between Ade and ......
questions.explanation: "Between" is a preposition and takes the object pronoun: "between Ade and me".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

The meeting was called ...... because the chairman was ill.
questions.explanation: To call off a meeting is to cancel it. Call up and call out have other meanings.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

The news from the war front ...... not encouraging.
questions.explanation: "News" is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb, despite its final s.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

The students were asked to ...... an essay on the dangers of drug abuse.
questions.explanation: In standard English one writes an essay. "Make an essay" is not idiomatic, and one carries out or performs a task, not an essay.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

If I ...... you, I would apologise to the elders.
questions.explanation: In unreal present conditions, standard English uses the past subjunctive "were" for every person: "If I were you". "Am" and "have been" do not fit an unreal condition, and "if I be" is archaic.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the underlined letter(s).

w__o__men
questions.explanation: The o in women is pronounced /ɪ/, as in sit. Wood has /ʊ/, moon /uː/ and wet /e/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the underlined letter(s).

c__ou__ntry
questions.explanation: The ou in country is /ʌ/, as in cut. Count has /aʊ/, court /ɔː/ and cot /ɒ/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the underlined letter(s).

h__ea__rt
questions.explanation: Heart has /ɑː/, the vowel of calm. Heard has /ɜː/, hear /ɪə/ and hat /æ/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the underlined letter(s).

__ch__ef
questions.explanation: The ch in chef is /ʃ/, as in machine. Chair and cheap have /tʃ/ and chemist has /k/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the underlined letter(s).

__th__ough
questions.explanation: Though begins with the voiced /ð/, as at the end of breathe. Breath and thick have the voiceless /θ/, and tea has /t/.

questions.stem: In which of the following words is the underlined letter silent?
questions.explanation: The b in debt is not pronounced: /det/. It is pronounced in number, amber and bulb.

questions.stem: Choose the word that rhymes with "bought".
questions.explanation: Bought and sort both have /ɔːt/. Bout has /aʊt/, boat /əʊt/ and but /ʌt/.

questions.stem: In the options, the syllable written in capital letters carries the primary stress. Choose the correct stress pattern for "examination".
questions.explanation: Words ending in -tion are stressed on the syllable just before the ending: ex-am-i-NA-tion.

questions.stem:
In the sentence below, the word in capital letters carries the emphatic stress. Choose the question the sentence answers.

"TUNDE wrote the letter."
questions.explanation: Stress on the subject, Tunde, answers a question about who did the action.

questions.stem: Which of these sentences is normally said with a rising tune at the end?
questions.explanation: Questions that can be answered yes or no normally end with a rising tune. Wh- questions, commands and statements normally fall.

questions.stem: According to the passage, fadama lands are valuable in the dry season because
options: they are close to large city markets
questions.explanation: After the flood recedes the land "stays moist long after the surrounding plains have turned brown and hard". The land does flood, which is how it gets its moisture.

questions.stem: Why do dry-season vegetables fetch good prices?
options: They are larger than rainy-season crops
questions.explanation: They "reach the market when little else is being harvested", so supply is low. Pumps are how they are watered, not why they sell well.

questions.stem: The word "recedes" as used in the passage means
questions.explanation: Floodwater that recedes withdraws from the land it covered. "Dries up" is tempting, but the passage says the water leaves moist soil behind, so it goes back rather than disappearing.

questions.stem: The writer mentions young people drifting to the cities in order to show that dry-season farming
options: is too hard for young people to do
questions.explanation: The practice "keeps young people employed in months that would otherwise be idle", which reduces the pressure to leave. It is a benefit to rural employment, not a complaint about cities.

questions.stem: The last paragraph is mainly concerned with
questions.explanation: It opens "The practice is not free of risk" and lists costly pumps, failing wells and competition with herders. History, crops and profits belong to earlier paragraphs.

questions.stem: Where did the bus break down?
questions.explanation: The passage says "somewhere past Onitsha, the engine coughed, spluttered and died". The bus had left Enugu and never reached Lagos in the passage.

questions.stem: "The engine coughed, spluttered and died" is an example of
questions.explanation: Coughing and dying are human actions given to an engine, which is personification. There is no "like" or "as", so it is not a simile, and nothing is exaggerated or self-contradictory.

questions.stem: The description of the driver staring into the engine suggests that he
options: was waiting for the engine to cool
did not know how to repair it
questions.explanation: He looks at it "with the expression of a man reading a letter in a language he did not know": he could not understand the fault. A mechanic later had to come.

questions.stem: The writer's attitude to the medicine seller is best described as
questions.explanation: Medicine that cures "anything from headaches to bad luck" is reported with quiet humour, which mocks the claim without anger.

questions.stem: By the end of the passage, Ifeoma's feelings had changed from
questions.explanation: "At first she fretted about arriving late", but after talking with the old woman she "had stopped worrying" and valued the journey. That is worry turning into contentment.

questions.stem: The passage mainly argues that
options: early lessons should use a familiar language
English should be banned from primary schools
parents should decide which language is taught
every Nigerian language needs textbooks now
questions.explanation: The writer supports teaching in the home language where a community shares one, while introducing English step by step. Banning English is never suggested.

questions.stem: Which of these is given as an objection to mother-tongue teaching?
options: Teachers refuse to learn new methods
Children forget their home language too quickly
questions.explanation: The opponents point out that a city classroom "may contain children who speak five or six" languages. The other options are not raised.

questions.stem: The writer's response to the objections is that they
questions.explanation: "These objections are real, but they are arguments for careful planning, not for abandoning the idea." The writer accepts them as real, so they are not called mistaken.

questions.stem: "Medium of instruction" as used in the passage means
options: the average level of a class
questions.explanation: A medium is the means by which something is passed on; the medium of instruction is the language teachers use in lessons.

questions.stem: The final sentence of the passage is meant mainly to
options: stress the child's need to understand
questions.explanation: It warns that no child should sit for years "understanding little of what is said", putting the child's understanding above every other concern. No teacher is blamed.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (1).
questions.explanation: Each house selects its best athletes and begins training them. Dismissing or rejecting them would leave nobody to train.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (2).
questions.explanation: Students who cannot run find other ways to help: banners, songs and the march past. "Compete" is tempting, but those activities are support, not competition.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (3).
questions.explanation: "Ablaze with colour" is a fixed expression for something very brightly coloured, matching the crowds, banners and drums. Empty and bare contradict the scene.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (4).
questions.explanation: "Can be heard far away" is the standard phrase. "Afar" is used in "from afar", and farther and further need a comparison.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (5).
questions.explanation: The outcome, the result, of the first race sets the mood for the day. Income, upkeep and overhead are not results of a race.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (6).
questions.explanation: After "are" in a passive sentence the past participle is needed: others "are beaten at the finishing line".

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (7).
questions.explanation: Learning to win and lose with dignity is sportsmanship. Craftsmanship, seamanship and showmanship are skills of other fields.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (8).
questions.explanation: A house that loses with dignity earns as much respect as one that wins with arrogance; respect is what dignity earns.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (9).
questions.explanation: At the end of a competition the trophy is presented to the winners. The other verbs do not suit a prize-giving.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (10).
questions.explanation: "But" contrasts the folded banners with the friendships, which endure, that is, last. Vanish and collapse would make "but" pointless.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"Ada has a soft spot for her youngest brother."
options: She shares a bedroom with him at home
She is often angry with him
She is especially fond of him
questions.explanation: To have a soft spot for someone is to be especially fond of them.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"The manager told the workers to bury the hatchet."
options: They should start a new project
questions.explanation: To bury the hatchet is to make peace and stop quarrelling. No tool is involved.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"Musa's argument does not hold water."
options: It is too long to follow
questions.explanation: An argument that does not hold water is unconvincing because it has weaknesses.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"The landlord's warning was a storm in a teacup."
options: A sudden change in the weather
A serious threat to the tenants
A secret plan to raise the rent
questions.explanation: A storm in a teacup is a lot of anger or excitement about something unimportant.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"Ngozi would rather walk than take a motorcycle."
options: She has no choice but to walk
questions.explanation: "Would rather" states a preference. It does not say she cannot afford a ride or has no choice.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The athlete was __exhausted__ after the long race.
questions.explanation: Exhausted means extremely tired.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The hunters moved __stealthily__ through the bush.
questions.explanation: Stealthily means quietly and secretly so as not to be noticed. Quickly is tempting but describes speed, not secrecy.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The committee's decision was __unanimous__.
questions.explanation: A unanimous decision is one every member agrees with.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

Bisi was __reluctant__ to lend her notes to her classmates.
questions.explanation: Reluctant means unwilling or hesitant. Eager is the opposite.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The elders described the young man's conduct as __impudent__.
questions.explanation: Impudent means disrespectful and rude, especially to elders.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The young man was __frugal__ with his first salary.
questions.explanation: Frugal means careful and sparing with money; the opposite is extravagant, spending freely and wastefully. Careful is close to frugal, not opposite.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The doctor said the disease was __contagious__.
questions.explanation: Contagious means spread by contact. Non-infectious is its opposite; incurable and life-threatening describe how serious a disease is, not how it spreads.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

Our team's victory was __decisive__.
questions.explanation: A decisive victory is won by a wide, clear margin. A narrow victory is only just won, so it is the opposite. Clear is a synonym.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The tenant was __punctual__ in paying his rent.
questions.explanation: Punctual means on time; the opposite is late.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The speaker's tone was __conciliatory__.
questions.explanation: A conciliatory tone tries to make peace. A hostile tone is the opposite.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

Each of the boys ...... given a new uniform.
questions.explanation: "Each" is singular, so the verb is singular: "Each of the boys was".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

Let's visit the museum tomorrow, ......?
questions.explanation: A suggestion with "let's" takes the tag "shall we?"

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

My uncle has lived in Kaduna ...... 2015.
questions.explanation: "Since" marks the point in time when something began; "for" is used with a length of time.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

I ...... my homework when the light went off.
questions.explanation: An action in progress interrupted by a past event takes the past continuous: "was doing".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

The bus took ...... hour to reach Jos.
questions.explanation: "Hour" begins with a vowel sound because the h is silent, so it takes "an". "Any hour" and "much hour" are not English.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

The children were told to behave ...... at the party.
questions.explanation: "Behave" takes a reflexive pronoun referring back to the subject: the children behave themselves. "Theirselves" is not standard English, and "behave them" is not English.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

The firefighters managed to put ...... the fire.
questions.explanation: To put out a fire is to extinguish it. "Put off" means postpone.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

Bread and butter ...... my favourite breakfast.
questions.explanation: "Bread and butter" names a single dish, so it takes a singular verb.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

The headmaster insisted on ...... the parents himself.
questions.explanation: A preposition such as "on" is followed by the -ing form: "insisted on meeting".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

The ...... of the bridge took three years.
questions.explanation: After "the" and before "of", a noun is needed: "construction".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the underlined letter(s).

s__ai__d
questions.explanation: Said is pronounced /sed/, with the vowel of bed. Laid has /eɪ/, side /aɪ/ and sad /æ/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the underlined letter(s).

b__oo__k
questions.explanation: Book has /ʊ/, as in put. Boot has /uː/, but /ʌ/ and bought /ɔː/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the underlined letter(s).

c__ow__
questions.explanation: Cow has the diphthong /aʊ/, as in plough. Cough has /ɒ/, though /əʊ/ and through /uː/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the underlined letter(s).

plea__s__ure
questions.explanation: The s in pleasure is /ʒ/, as in vision. Pressure and sure have /ʃ/ and pleasant has /z/.

questions.stem: In which of the following words is the final -ed pronounced /ɪd/?
questions.explanation: After /t/ or /d/, -ed is pronounced /ɪd/: wanted. Walked and laughed end in /t/ and played in /d/.

questions.stem: Choose the word that rhymes with "through".
questions.explanation: Through and shoe both end in /uː/. Though has /əʊ/, tough /ʌf/ and trough /ɒf/.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is stressed on the second syllable?
questions.explanation: Begin is be-GIN. Garden, window and father are all stressed on the first syllable.

questions.stem: In the options, the syllable written in capital letters carries the primary stress. Choose the correct stress pattern for "comfortable".
questions.explanation: Comfortable is stressed on its first syllable, COM. In everyday speech the second syllable is often reduced, but the stress never moves to it.

questions.stem:
In the sentence below, the word in capital letters carries the emphatic stress. Choose the question the sentence answers.

"The bus left at SIX o'clock."
options: Did the bus arrive at six o'clock?
Did the bus leave at five o'clock?
Did the train leave at six o'clock?
questions.explanation: The emphasis on SIX corrects a wrong time, so the sentence answers a question that got the hour wrong.

questions.stem:
In the sentence below, the word in capital letters carries the emphatic stress. Choose the question the sentence answers.

"Amina is reading in the LIBRARY."
options: Is Musa reading in the library?
Is Amina reading in the classroom?
Is Amina writing in the library?
Was Amina reading in the library?
questions.explanation: Stress on LIBRARY corrects the place, so it answers a question that named another place.

questions.stem: The passage mainly compares
options: the rulers of the past and of the present
old and modern ways of spreading news
questions.explanation: It describes the town crier, then today's phones, and draws a lesson from the comparison. The gong and the well are details within it.

questions.stem: Which of these is given as a limit of the town crier system?
options: The crier refused to answer questions
Messages changed as they were retold
Only the ruler could hear the news
The gong could not be heard at dusk
questions.explanation: A message "changed a little each time it was retold" and could reach only as far as the crier walked. Answering questions is listed as a strength.

questions.stem: According to the writer, an advantage of the town crier over modern phones was
options: people no longer needed the market
questions.explanation: The crier was known and carried the palace's authority, whereas today "no one stands at the doorway to answer questions or take responsibility". Speed belongs to the phone.

questions.stem: The word "authority" as used in the passage means
questions.explanation: The crier's words "carried the authority of the palace": they had the ruler's official power behind them.

questions.stem: The writer ends the passage by
options: praising the speed of modern phones
urging caution before passing on news
calling for the return of town criers
questions.explanation: The last sentence recommends the old listener's habit of asking who sent a message and why before repeating it. The writer does not ask for criers to return.

questions.stem: During his first three months, Musa
questions.explanation: "He swept the floor, sharpened chisels and carried planks" and was "not allowed to touch a saw".

questions.stem: "A tree does not bear fruit in the season it is planted" is
questions.explanation: It is a traditional saying that teaches a general truth, patience, through a picture from nature. That is a proverb.

questions.stem: Musa was able to repair the chair because he had
questions.explanation: "He had watched closely while he swept, and he knew how the joints should fit." His menial work had been a hidden lesson.

questions.stem: By giving Musa the small chisel, Alhaji Danladi showed
options: that he was leaving the workshop
questions.explanation: It was the chisel "he never lent to anyone", and he says "Tomorrow you begin": he now trusted Musa with real work.

questions.stem: "Musa was not comforted" suggests that he
questions.explanation: Not being comforted means his mother's words did not ease his frustration. Nothing says he cried or planned to leave.

questions.stem: The writer believes that the main problem is
options: a lack of interest in reading
questions.explanation: "What is lacking is not the desire to read but easy access to books." The writer rejects the idea that people do not want to read.

questions.stem: The writer mentions drivers at motor parks to show that
questions.explanation: The examples of drivers and worshippers are given to answer the charge that Nigerians do not read.

questions.stem: The writer prefers small community libraries to grand buildings because they
questions.explanation: Small libraries "can do more than a grand building that few can reach": the point is nearness to readers.

questions.stem: The tone of the last paragraph is
questions.explanation: The writer says the plan needs no great wealth and that the returns "will repay the effort many times over", which is hopeful.

questions.stem: The word "acquire" as used in the passage means
questions.explanation: A habit that every child can acquire is one every child can develop. "Purchase" is another sense of acquire but does not fit a habit.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (1).
questions.explanation: Members agree to pay a fixed sum at regular intervals, which builds the amount given to one member each time.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (2).
questions.explanation: "Each time the whole amount is given to one member in turn" means the members take it one after another, and the next sentence confirms that everyone receives it once.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (3).
questions.explanation: A system that depends on trust needs trust in order to work, which the next sentences explain. "Consists of" takes a different preposition, and "insists on" or "remarks on" need a person as subject.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (4).
questions.explanation: To default on a duty or a debt is to fail to pay it. A member who defaults loses respect; insisting on or reflecting on a duty would not.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (5).
questions.explanation: Few groups will admit, let in, a known defaulter again. Ignore, praise and describe do not make sense with "again" here.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (6).
questions.explanation: The group compels members to set money aside when they might spend it. The other verbs mean stopping them, which contradicts the paragraph.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (7).
questions.explanation: A large sum received at once can be invested wisely, for example in stock for a shop. "Wasted wisely" contradicts itself.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (8).
questions.explanation: Groups now remind members of their payments by text message. Punishing or replacing members by text does not fit the friendly tone.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (9).
questions.explanation: The principle, the basic idea, remains the same. Principal is a head of school or a sum of money, and principled is an adjective.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best fills gap (10).
questions.explanation: The passage has shown that the system "depends on trust"; trust and discipline are what achieve a great deal.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"The two companies are now at loggerheads."
options: They have joined together as one company
questions.explanation: To be at loggerheads is to be in strong disagreement.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"The headmaster's decision was the last straw for the teachers."
options: It was the final cause of their anger
It was the least important decision of all
It was their last chance to protest
questions.explanation: The last straw is the final small problem that makes a situation unbearable after many others.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"Tunde has burnt his boats with his former employers."
options: He has paid all his debts
He has started a rival business
He cannot go back to them
questions.explanation: To burn one's boats is to act in a way that makes return impossible.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"The pastor called a spade a spade."
options: He spoke about tools used in farming
questions.explanation: To call a spade a spade is to speak frankly, without softening the truth.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"Funmi's success in the examination was a feather in her cap."
options: It was a matter of pure luck
It was a reward from her school
It made her proud and rude
questions.explanation: A feather in one's cap is an achievement one can be proud of.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"The suspect was given the benefit of the doubt."
options: He was released after paying a fine
He was found guilty at once
questions.explanation: To give someone the benefit of the doubt is to accept their account because it cannot be proved false.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"The project was nipped in the bud."
options: It was stopped at an early stage
It was completed well ahead of time
questions.explanation: To nip something in the bud is to stop it before it can develop.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"Amaka is no longer the shy girl she used to be."
options: She was shy in the past
questions.explanation: "No longer" and "used to be" together mean she was shy before but is not now.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"Hardly had the meeting started when the lights went off."
options: The lights failed just after it began
The lights went off long before it began
The meeting was hard to start
questions.explanation: "Hardly ... when" means one thing happened immediately after another: the meeting had just started when the lights failed.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

"The committee's report was swept under the carpet."
options: It was cleaned up and reissued
questions.explanation: To sweep something under the carpet is to hide or ignore it so that it is not dealt with.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The pupils were asked to __commence__ writing.
questions.explanation: Commence means begin.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The judge was __impartial__ throughout the trial.
questions.explanation: Impartial means not favouring either side, that is, fair.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The clerk kept __meticulous__ records of every payment.
questions.explanation: Meticulous means showing great attention to detail, that is, very careful. Untidy is the opposite.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The village head __reprimanded__ the boys for fighting.
questions.explanation: To reprimand is to rebuke or scold formally. Punished is close but means imposing a penalty, which reprimand does not require.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The drought led to a __scarcity__ of food in the region.
questions.explanation: Scarcity means a shortage. Surplus is its opposite.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The lawyer's argument was __cogent__.
questions.explanation: A cogent argument is clear, logical and convincing.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The general was known for his __candour__.
questions.explanation: Candour is the quality of being open and honest in speech: frankness.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

We must __curb__ the spread of malaria in our community.
questions.explanation: To curb is to restrain or control.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The road to the village is __narrow__.
questions.explanation: Narrow is the opposite of wide.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The new policy was __beneficial__ to the farmers.
questions.explanation: Beneficial means helpful; the opposite is harmful.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The prefect was __diligent__ in carrying out his duties.
questions.explanation: Diligent means hardworking and careful; the opposite is lazy.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The crowd was __hostile__ to the visitors.
questions.explanation: Hostile means unfriendly; its opposite is friendly. Indifferent means not caring either way, which is not the opposite.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The supply of drugs to the clinic was __erratic__.
questions.explanation: Erratic means irregular and unpredictable; the opposite is regular. Adequate is about quantity, not pattern.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

The minister's reply was __ambiguous__.
questions.explanation: An ambiguous reply can be understood in more than one way. A clear reply has only one obvious meaning.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word or phrase.

Kemi's interest in music is __genuine__.
questions.explanation: Genuine means real. Feigned means pretended, the opposite.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

The number of students in the hall ...... increasing.
questions.explanation: "The number of" takes a singular verb; "a number of" would take a plural one.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

I am your best friend, ......?
questions.explanation: The standard tag after "I am" is "aren't I?"

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

You hardly ever visit us, ......?
questions.explanation: "Hardly" makes the sentence negative, so the tag is positive: "do you?"

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

The teacher was angry ...... the students for coming late.
questions.explanation: In standard British English one is angry with a person and angry about a thing.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

He was accused ...... stealing the goat.
questions.explanation: The verb "accuse" takes "of": accused of stealing.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

If it rains tomorrow, we ...... the match.
questions.explanation: A real future condition takes the present in the if-clause and "will" in the main clause.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

If she had studied harder, she ...... the examination.
questions.explanation: The third conditional pairs "had studied" with "would have passed".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

This is the ...... book I have ever read.
questions.explanation: "Ever" with a single item compared against all others needs the superlative: "the most interesting".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

The farmer bought three ...... at the market.
questions.explanation: "Sheep" has the same form in the singular and the plural.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

The children were told to look ...... their younger brother.
questions.explanation: To look after someone is to take care of them. Look into means investigate.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

The scissors ...... on the table where you left them.
questions.explanation: "Scissors" is a plural noun with no singular form, so it takes a plural verb, as "them" confirms. "A pair of scissors" would take "is".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

He said that he ...... to Ibadan the following day.
questions.explanation: In reported speech after a past reporting verb, "will" shifts back to "would".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

The government has ...... a ban on the import of the drug.
questions.explanation: A ban is imposed. "Made a ban" and "done a ban" are not standard collocations.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

The ...... of the house was completed in December.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is "painting": paint plus -ing, with no doubled consonant.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.

The judge listened ...... to both sides of the argument.
questions.explanation: "Listened" is a verb, so an adverb is needed: "patiently".

questions.stem:

b__u__sy
questions.explanation: Busy is /ˈbɪzi/, with the vowel of pin. Bus has /ʌ/, bush /ʊ/ and boot /uː/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the underlined letter(s).

p__ea__r
questions.explanation: Pear has /eə/, as in care. Peer has /ɪə/, purr /ɜː/ and pure /ʊə/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the underlined letter(s).

s__ew__
questions.explanation: Sew is pronounced like so, with /əʊ/ as in go. Few and new have /uː/ and saw has /ɔː/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the underlined letter(s).

bl__oo__d
questions.explanation: Blood has /ʌ/, the vowel of love. Food has /uː/, good /ʊ/ and load /əʊ/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the underlined letter(s).

m__a__ny
questions.explanation: Many is /ˈmeni/, with the vowel of friend. Main has /eɪ/, man /æ/ and mine /aɪ/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the underlined letter(s).

w__or__d
questions.explanation: Word has /ɜː/, as in bird. Ward and worn have /ɔː/ and wood has /ʊ/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the underlined letter(s).

__ph__oto
questions.explanation: The ph in photo is /f/, the sound of gh in laugh. In shepherd the ph is /p/, though has a silent gh and ghost has /ɡ/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the underlined letter(s).

a__ss__ure
questions.explanation: The ss in assure is /ʃ/, as in sugar. Assist and sauce have /s/ and dessert has /z/.

questions.stem: Choose the word in which the underlined letter is not pronounced.
questions.explanation: The k in knock is silent: /nɒk/. It is pronounced in kettle, break and key.

questions.stem: In which of the following words is the final -es or -s pronounced /ɪz/?
questions.explanation: After /tʃ/ the ending is /ɪz/: watches. Boys and rides end in /z/ and caps in /s/.

questions.stem: Choose the word that rhymes with "heard".
questions.explanation: Heard and bird both have /ɜːd/. Beard has /ɪəd/, hard /ɑːd/ and head /ed/.

questions.stem: Which pair of words is pronounced the same?
questions.explanation: Flour and flower are both /ˈflaʊə/. The other pairs differ in their vowels.

questions.stem: In the options, the syllable written in capital letters carries the primary stress. Choose the correct stress pattern for "photographer".
questions.explanation: Photographer is stressed on the second syllable, although photograph is stressed on the first.

questions.stem: Which of the following words has a different stress pattern from the others?
questions.explanation: Hotel is stressed on the second syllable, ho-TEL; table, paper and doctor are stressed on the first.

questions.stem:
In the sentence below, the word in capital letters carries the emphatic stress. Choose the question the sentence answers.

"My sister WALKED to school."
options: Did your sister walk to church?
Did your sister drive to school?
Did your brother walk to school?
questions.explanation: Stress on WALKED corrects the way she travelled, so it answers a question about another means of transport.
